claim: Shisa7 shares high structural similarity with Shisa6 and Shisa9.
source: Shisa7 shares high structural similarity with the established AMPAR-associated proteins Shisa6, and Shisa9 (Figure 1a).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by Figure 1a showing structural comparison

claim: Shisa7 gene is abundantly expressed in the mouse brain.
source: Real-time PCR showed abundant expression of the Shisa7 gene in the mouse brain, where it is expressed with a profile similar to AMPAR genes Gria1 and Gria2 during postnatal development (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Shisa7 expression profile during postnatal development is similar to AMPAR genes Gria1 and Gria2.
source: Real-time PCR showed abundant expression of the Shisa7 gene in the mouse brain, where it is expressed with a profile similar to AMPAR genes Gria1 and Gria2 during postnatal development (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by real-time PCR data comparing expression profiles

claim: Shisa7 shows widespread expression in the whole brain except for the cerebellum.
source: In situ hybridization analysis (Allen Brain Atlas; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) revealed widespread expression in the whole brain, except for the cerebellum, with high expression in cortex, striatum, amygdala and hippocampus CA1-3 and dentate gyrus, as was shown previously (Farrow et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data from Allen Brain Atlas and cited previous work

claim: Shisa7 shows high expression in cortex, striatum, amygdala and hippocampus CA1-3 and dentate gyrus.
source: In situ hybridization analysis (Allen Brain Atlas; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) revealed widespread expression in the whole brain, except for the cerebellum, with high expression in cortex, striatum, amygdala and hippocampus CA1-3 and dentate gyrus, as was shown previously (Farrow et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data and cited previous work

claim: The Shisa7 antibody is specific for Shisa7 protein.
source: A Shisa7 knockout (KO) mouse was generated, which confirmed the specificity of the Shisa7 antibody (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Confirmed by absence of signal in KO mice shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Shisa7 protein is highly enriched in the cortex.
source: Immunoblotting with this antibody showed highly enriched expression of Shisa7 in the cortex, as well as expression in striatum and hippocampus (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1b

claim: Shisa7 protein is expressed in striatum and hippocampus.
source: Immunoblotting with this antibody showed highly enriched expression of Shisa7 in the cortex, as well as expression in striatum and hippocampus (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1b

claim: Shisa7 protein in the hippocampus is glycosylated.
source: The Shisa7 protein in the hippocampus is glycosylated (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) leading to an increase in observed molecular weight, similar to Shisa6 (Klaassen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by PNGase-F treatment data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and comparison to Shisa6

claim: Glycosylation of Shisa7 leads to an increase in observed molecular weight.
source: The Shisa7 protein in the hippocampus is glycosylated (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) leading to an increase in observed molecular weight, similar to Shisa6 (Klaassen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by molecular weight shift data and comparison to Shisa6

claim: Shisa7 shows a moderately high level of granular staining along dendrites.
source: A qualitative analysis of Shisa7 localization showed a moderately high level of granular staining for Shisa7 present along the dendrites, co-localizing with a similar granular staining for the synaptic protein Homer1 (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 1c

claim: Shisa7 co-localizes with the synaptic protein Homer1.
source: A qualitative analysis of Shisa7 localization showed a moderately high level of granular staining for Shisa7 present along the dendrites, co-localizing with a similar granular staining for the synaptic protein Homer1 (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by co-localization imaging in Figure 1c

claim: Overexpression of Shisa7 causes considerable spine loss in both Shisa7 KO and WT neurons.
source: A quantitative analysis was not possible, as we observed considerable spine loss after overexpression of Shisa7 in Shisa7 KO and WT alike.
evidence: Directly observed experimental result

claim: Shisa7 is highly enriched in the Triton-X100-insoluble postsynaptic density (PSD) fraction.
source: In agreement with the co-localization of Shisa7 and Homer1, subcellular fractionation of hippocampal proteins revealed that Shisa7 was highly enriched in the Triton-X100-insoluble postsynaptic density (PSD) fraction, in which it co-purified with PSD-95, GluA2 and GluN2A (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 1d

claim: Shisa7 co-purifies with PSD-95, GluA2 and GluN2A in the PSD fraction.
source: In agreement with the co-localization of Shisa7 and Homer1, subcellular fractionation of hippocampal proteins revealed that Shisa7 was highly enriched in the Triton-X100-insoluble postsynaptic density (PSD) fraction, in which it co-purified with PSD-95, GluA2 and GluN2A (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 1d

claim: Shisa7 is an AMPAR-interacting protein in HEK293 cells without subunit specificity.
source: Shisa7 is an AMPAR-interacting protein in HEK293 cells without subunit specificity (Figure 1e).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in HEK293 cells shown in Figure 1e

claim: Shisa7 binds directly to homomeric GluA1, GluA2 and GluA3 receptors in HEK293 cells.
source: Precipitation of Flag-Shisa7 (~60 kDa) from HEK293 cells using a Flag antibody shows that upon co-expression it binds directly to homomeric GluA1, GluA2 and GluA3 receptors, whereas having minimal affinity for GluK2.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1e

claim: Shisa7 has minimal affinity for GluK2.
source: Precipitation of Flag-Shisa7 (~60 kDa) from HEK293 cells using a Flag antibody shows that upon co-expression it binds directly to homomeric GluA1, GluA2 and GluA3 receptors, whereas having minimal affinity for GluK2.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing weak or absent binding in Figure 1e

claim: Shisa7 forms a stable association with AMPAR subunits GluA1, GluA2, and GluA3 in native hippocampal complexes.
source: Under these conditions, Shisa7 formed a stable association with AMPAR subunits GluA1, GluA2, and GluA3 (Table 1, Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data from native hippocampal immunoprecipitation shown in Table 1

claim: Shisa6 is identified in native hippocampal Shisa7 complexes.
source: Based on the established AMPAR interactome (Schwenk et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2014), we furthermore identified Shisa6 in these native Shisa7 complexes.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data from immunoprecipitation and cited AMPAR interactome studies

claim: PSD-95 is the most prominent PDZ domain-containing interactor in native hippocampal Shisa7 complexes.
source: Mass spectrometry of native hippocampal Shisa7 complexes identified PSD-95 as the most prominent PDZ domain-containing interactor (Table 1), and the direct nature of this interaction was confirmed by direct two-hybrid assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data in Table 1 and two-hybrid assay in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The interaction between Shisa7 and PSD-95 is direct.
source: Mass spectrometry of native hippocampal Shisa7 complexes identified PSD-95 as the most prominent PDZ domain-containing interactor (Table 1), and the direct nature of this interaction was confirmed by direct two-hybrid assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Confirmed by direct two-hybrid assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The association between Shisa7 and PSD-95 is dependent on the Shisa7 type II PDZ-ligand motif (EVTV).
source: Finally, we established that the association between Shisa7 and PSD-95 is dependent on the Shisa7 type II PDZ-ligand motif (EVTV; Figure 1—figure supplement 2), similar as was reported for Shisa9 (Karataeva et al., 2014) and Shisa6 (Klaassen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by two-hybrid assay with EVTV deletion mutant in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and cited studies on Shisa9 and Shisa6

claim: Shisa7 did not affect AMPAR deactivation in HEK293 cells.
source: Similar to that study, we can confirm here that in our hands Shisa7 did not affect most properties of fast glutamate application (1 ms; 1 mM) on AMPARs in HEK293 cells. Co-expression of Shisa7 did not alter AMPAR deactivation, rise time, or rectification (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), in contrast to Shisa6 (Klaassen et al., 2016) and Shisa9 (von Engelhardt et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in HEK293 cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and comparison to cited studies

claim: Shisa7 did not alter AMPAR rise time in HEK293 cells.
source: Similar to that study, we can confirm here that in our hands Shisa7 did not affect most properties of fast glutamate application (1 ms; 1 mM) on AMPARs in HEK293 cells. Co-expression of Shisa7 did not alter AMPAR deactivation, rise time, or rectification (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), in contrast to Shisa6 (Klaassen et al., 2016) and Shisa9 (von Engelhardt et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in HEK293 cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Shisa7 did not alter AMPAR rectification in HEK293 cells.
source: Similar to that study, we can confirm here that in our hands Shisa7 did not affect most properties of fast glutamate application (1 ms; 1 mM) on AMPARs in HEK293 cells. Co-expression of Shisa7 did not alter AMPAR deactivation, rise time, or rectification (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), in contrast to Shisa6 (Klaassen et al., 2016) and Shisa9 (von Engelhardt et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by IV-curve data in HEK293 cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Shisa7 significantly affects desensitization time upon prolonged glutamate application in HEK293 cells.
source: Yet, Shisa7 had a significant effect in lowering desensitization properties upon prolonged glutamate application (1 s, 1 mM; Figure 2a,b) of homomeric AMPARs, i.e., on the desensitization time (t-test; p=0.007) and steady state current (t-test; p=0.012).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2a,b

claim: Shisa7 significantly affects steady state current upon prolonged glutamate application in HEK293 cells.
source: Yet, Shisa7 had a significant effect in lowering desensitization properties upon prolonged glutamate application (1 s, 1 mM; Figure 2a,b) of homomeric AMPARs, i.e., on the desensitization time (t-test; p=0.007) and steady state current (t-test; p=0.012).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2a,b

claim: Shisa7 slows down recovery from desensitization in HEK293 cells.
source: In addition, Shisa7 affected the recovery from desensitization using two consecutive 1 ms glutamate (1 mM) applications with variable time interval (Figure 2c,d). Shisa7 slowed down recovery from desensitization, resulting in an increase in the time constant of recovery(τrecovery: 82.6 ± 6.7 ms (GluA1) vs. 119.1 ± 10.9 ms (GluA1 +Shisa7); t-test; p=0.006; Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by paired-pulse recovery data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2c,d

claim: Shisa7 increases the time constant of recovery from desensitization from 82.6 ± 6.7 ms to 119.1 ± 10.9 ms in HEK293 cells.
source: Shisa7 slowed down recovery from desensitization, resulting in an increase in the time constant of recovery(τrecovery: 82.6 ± 6.7 ms (GluA1) vs. 119.1 ± 10.9 ms (GluA1 +Shisa7); t-test; p=0.006; Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by quantitative electrophysiology data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2d

claim: Lack of Shisa7 results in faster deactivation kinetics of AMPARs in CA1 pyramidal cells.
source: In WT pyramidal neurons, the decay of mEPSCs was slower than in Shisa7 KO (7.48 ± 0.22 vs. 5.54 ± 0.07, unpaired t-test, p<0.001), whereas rise time, amplitude, and frequency were similar between WT and Shisa7 KO (MWU-test, p=0.462; unpaired t-test, p=0.297; MWU-test, p=0.469, respectively).
evidence: Supported by mEPSC recordings with statistical analysis

claim: Lack of Shisa7 does not affect mEPSC rise time, amplitude, or frequency in CA1 pyramidal cells.
source: In WT pyramidal neurons, the decay of mEPSCs was slower than in Shisa7 KO (7.48 ± 0.22 vs. 5.54 ± 0.07, unpaired t-test, p<0.001), whereas rise time, amplitude, and frequency were similar between WT and Shisa7 KO (MWU-test, p=0.462; unpaired t-test, p=0.297; MWU-test, p=0.469, respectively).
evidence: Supported by mEPSC recordings with statistical analysis showing no significant differences

claim: Lack of Shisa7 does not affect series resistance or resting membrane potential in CA1 pyramidal cells.
source: In addition, basic neurophysiological parameters were not affected (series resistance 141 ± 12 vs. 130±13 MΩ, unpaired t-test, p=0.541 and resting membrane potential: −70.7 ± 1.2 vs. −71.9 ± 3.8 mV, unpaired t-test, p=0.768; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology measurements with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Absence of Shisa7 does not induce changes in the abundance of membrane-localized AMPARs or their core interactors.
source: To confirm that a lack of Shisa7 did not induce changes in the abundance of membrane-localized AMPARs (or their core interactors), similar to what was observed for Shisa6 (Klaassen et al., 2016), immunoblotting of the hippocampal synaptic membrane fraction from Shisa7 WT and KO mice was performed. This revealed no difference in the levels of (subunits of) the AMPAR, NMDAR, PSD-95, TARPs, CNIH, Shisa9 or Shisa6 present at the synapse (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and comparison to cited Shisa6 study

claim: Synaptic GluA2 expression is similar in Shisa7 KO and WT hippocampal neurons at DIV14 and DIV21.
source: Also, the expression of synaptic GluA2, as defined by punctate expression of Homer1, in the absence of Shisa7 (Figure 4b,c) was similar (DIV14: 1.00 ± 0.04 vs. 1.02 ± 0.05; DIV21: 1.00 ± 0.03 vs. 1.10 ± 0.10), albeit that there was between culture variation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry quantification shown in Figure 4b,c

claim: There is no difference in input-output curves of AMPAR eEPSCs between WT and Shisa7 KO brain slices.
source: There was no difference in input-output curves of AMPAR eEPSCs between WT and Shisa7 KO brain slices (p=0.126; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by input-output curve analysis with statistical test shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Shisa7 KO currents show a smaller decay tau for evoked EPSCs compared to WT.
source: Similar to the observation made for mEPSCs, the decay kinetics of these evoked EPSCs were significantly different, with Shisa7 KO currents showing a smaller decay tau (16.9 ± 1.4 vs. 12.0 ± 0.9, MWU-test, p=0.006; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by evoked EPSC recordings with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Shisa7 KO shows a faster rise time for evoked EPSCs compared to WT.
source: In addition, a faster rise time (2.80 ± 0.26 vs. 2.00 ± 0.13; MWU-test, p=0.023; Figure 5—figure supplement 1) was observed in the Shisa7 KO.
evidence: Supported by evoked EPSC recordings with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The effect of Shisa7 deletion on EPSC kinetics is specific for AMPARs and not NMDARs.
source: This effect was specific for the AMPAR, as the amplitude, rise and decay time was similar between Shisa7 KO and WT animals for evoked NMDAR currents, while blocking AMPAR currents (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by NMDAR current recordings showing no differences, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Shisa7 does not affect paired-pulse ratios at any stimulation frequency tested.
source: We did not observe a difference in the paired-pulse ratios at any stimulation frequency (e.g., 20 Hz; MWU-test, p=0.439; Figure 5b–e).
evidence: Supported by paired-pulse ratio measurements at multiple frequencies with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5b-e

claim: Shisa7 does not affect synaptic depression during stimulation trains at 5, 20 or 50 Hz.
source: Similarly, with stimulation trains of 10 pulses at 5, 20 or 50 Hz (Figure 5c–e), we did not observe a change in synaptic depression.
evidence: Supported by train stimulation data shown in Figure 5c-e

claim: Unlike Shisa9 and Shisa6, Shisa7 does not affect short-term synaptic plasticity.
source: Thus, unlike Shisa9 and Shisa6, Shisa7 does not affect short-term synaptic plasticity.
evidence: Inferred from lack of effects on paired-pulse ratios and synaptic depression, contrasted with cited effects of Shisa9 and Shisa6

claim: TARP γ-8 is necessary for long-term potentiation of hippocampal glutamatergic synapses.
source: Whereas TARP γ−8 is necessary for long-term potentiation of hippocampal glutamatergic synapses (Rouach et al., 2005), with specifically phosphorylation of S277/S281 being important for LTP as well as associative learning (Park et al., 2016), Shisa9 does not have such a role (Khodosevich et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from previous studies on TARP γ-8

claim: Phosphorylation of TARP γ-8 at S277/S281 is important for LTP and associative learning.
source: Whereas TARP γ−8 is necessary for long-term potentiation of hippocampal glutamatergic synapses (Rouach et al., 2005), with specifically phosphorylation of S277/S281 being important for LTP as well as associative learning (Park et al., 2016), Shisa9 does not have such a role (Khodosevich et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from previous study on TARP γ-8 phosphorylation

claim: Shisa9 does not have a role in long-term potentiation.
source: Whereas TARP γ−8 is necessary for long-term potentiation of hippocampal glutamatergic synapses (Rouach et al., 2005), with specifically phosphorylation of S277/S281 being important for LTP as well as associative learning (Park et al., 2016), Shisa9 does not have such a role (Khodosevich et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from previous study on Shisa9

claim: Shisa7 KO mice show a decrease in the maintenance phase of hippocampal LTP compared with WT littermates.
source: Shisa7 KO mice showed a decrease in the maintenance phase of hippocampal LTP compared with WT littermates (Figure 6a; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by LTP recordings shown in Figure 6a and Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Synaptic potentiation is lower in Shisa7 KO animals between 20 to 25 minutes after LTP induction.
source: Synaptic potentiation was lower in Shisa7 KO animals between 20 to 25 minutes (WT (n = 5): 1.81 ± 0.16; KO (n = 6): 1.10 ± 0.11; unpaired t-test, p=0.004), and 25 to 30 minutes (WT: 1.84 ± 0.16; KO: 1.17 ± 0.06; unpaired t-test, p=0.004; Figure 6b, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by quantified LTP data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6b

claim: Synaptic potentiation is lower in Shisa7 KO animals between 25 to 30 minutes after LTP induction.
source: Synaptic potentiation was lower in Shisa7 KO animals between 20 to 25 minutes (WT (n = 5): 1.81 ± 0.16; KO (n = 6): 1.10 ± 0.11; unpaired t-test, p=0.004), and 25 to 30 minutes (WT: 1.84 ± 0.16; KO: 1.17 ± 0.06; unpaired t-test, p=0.004; Figure 6b, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by quantified LTP data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6b

claim: The initiation of LTP is significantly affected in Shisa7 KO animals.
source: In addition, the initiation of LTP was also significantly affected as apparent in the first 5 minutes after stimulation (0–5'; WT (n = 5): 2.46 ± 0.41; KO (n = 6): 1.52 ± 0.17; unpaired t-test p=0.049).
evidence: Supported by quantified LTP data with statistical analysis

claim: A genotype effect is detected during the first three 10 s measurements immediately after LTP induction.
source: In fact, during the first three 10 s measurements immediately after LTP induction, a genotype effect was detected (unpaired t-tests, p=0.057; p=0.034; p=0.077, respectively; Figure 6c).
evidence: Supported by high temporal resolution LTP data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6c

claim: Both WT and Shisa7 KO genotypes show induction of LTP in the 5 minutes following theta burst stimulation.
source: Compared with the first 5 minutes of their baseline recordings, both genotypes showed induction of LTP in the 5 minutes following theta burst stimulation (Figure 6a), however, this was more pronounced in WT animals (paired t-test, WT: p=0.004; KO: p=0.010).
evidence: Supported by LTP data comparing baseline to post-stimulation with statistical analysis

claim: LTP induction is more pronounced in WT animals compared to Shisa7 KO.
source: Compared with the first 5 minutes of their baseline recordings, both genotypes showed induction of LTP in the 5 minutes following theta burst stimulation (Figure 6a), however, this was more pronounced in WT animals (paired t-test, WT: p=0.004; KO: p=0.010).
evidence: Supported by comparison of LTP magnitude between genotypes with statistical analysis

claim: Glycine-induced chemical LTP increases the number of surface GluA1 spots in WT neurons.
source: At ~15 minutes after a brief application of glycine in WT neurons, the number of GluA1 spots was significantly increased at the surface compared with non-stimulated cells (t-test; p<0.001, Figure 6e; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry quantification with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6e

claim: In Shisa7 KO neurons, the number of surface GluA1 spots is not increased after chemical LTP.
source: In line with the electrophysiological data, in Shisa7 KO neurons the number of surface GluA1 spots was not increased, suggesting that recruitment of AMPARs at the surface was hampered (MWU test, p=0.894, Figure 6e; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry quantification with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6e

claim: Recruitment of AMPARs at the surface is hampered in Shisa7 KO neurons during LTP.
source: In line with the electrophysiological data, in Shisa7 KO neurons the number of surface GluA1 spots was not increased, suggesting that recruitment of AMPARs at the surface was hampered (MWU test, p=0.894, Figure 6e; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Inferred from lack of increase in surface GluA1 after chemical LTP in KO neurons

claim: Shisa7 KO mice show a deficit in short-term contextual fear memory (2 hr after conditioning).
source: Shisa7 KO mice showed a deficit in memory expression both at 2 hr (WT (n = 8): 45.3 ± 2.9%; KO (n = 7): 14.0 ± 2.86%; unpaired t-test, p<0.001), and at 24 hr after conditioning (WT (n = 9): 33.0 ± 5.2%; KO (n = 10): 9.2 ± 1.8%; MWU test, p<0.001) (Figure 7a–d, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by contextual fear conditioning data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 7a-d

claim: Shisa7 KO mice show a deficit in long-term contextual fear memory (24 hr after conditioning).
source: Shisa7 KO mice showed a deficit in memory expression both at 2 hr (WT (n = 8): 45.3 ± 2.9%; KO (n = 7): 14.0 ± 2.86%; unpaired t-test, p<0.001), and at 24 hr after conditioning (WT (n = 9): 33.0 ± 5.2%; KO (n = 10): 9.2 ± 1.8%; MWU test, p<0.001) (Figure 7a–d, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by contextual fear conditioning data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 7c-d

claim: There is no genotype difference in baseline locomotor activity between Shisa7 KO and WT mice.
source: There was no genotype difference in base line locomotor activity (unpaired t-tests p=0.245) or shock perception (unpaired t-tests p=0.573).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity measurements with statistical analysis

claim: There is no genotype difference in shock perception between Shisa7 KO and WT mice.
source: There was no genotype difference in base line locomotor activity (unpaired t-tests p=0.245) or shock perception (unpaired t-tests p=0.573).
evidence: Supported by velocity measurements during shock with statistical analysis

claim: Shisa7 KO mice do not display altered locomotor activity in the open field test.
source: Together with locomotor data in a novel environment, i.e., distance moved in the open field test, our data indicate that Shisa7 KO mice did not display altered locomotor activity (unpaired t-test p=0.106; Figure 7—figure supplement 2) or a difference in sensing the shock that might have confounded the acquisition and expression of fear memory.
evidence: Supported by open field test data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2

claim: Shisa7 is expressed in the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeA).
source: Shisa7 shows a widespread expression pattern throughout the brain, including the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeA; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The central nucleus of the amygdala is important for consolidation and expression of fear memory.
source: Given the importance of the CeA in consolidation and expression of fear memory (Wilensky et al., 2006; Ciocchi et al., 2010), plasticity-related deficits by deletion of Shisa7 might disturb US-CS acquisition and subsequent expression of fear, independently of hippocampal plasticity.
evidence: Cited from previous studies on CeA function

claim: Auditory fear conditioning is not affected in Shisa7 KO mice.
source: Upon presentation of the tone, both KO and WT mice showed increased levels of freezing (WT: 31.7 ± 6.6%; KO: 41.3 ± 8.8%; Figure 7e,f) (factorial repeated measure ANOVA for switching on the tone, F(1,22)=27.80; p<0.001), with no genotype difference (F(1,22)=0.98; p=0.334), and lack of tone x genotype interaction (F(1,22)=0.47; p=0.500; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by auditory fear conditioning data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 7e-f

claim: Shisa7 KO mice show low levels of freezing in a novel context before tone presentation.
source: After conditioning, mice were tested in a novel context, in which they showed low levels of freezing (WT (n = 13): 10.7 ± 2.4%; KO (n = 11): 13.9 ± 2.9%; unpaired t-test, p=0.385)).
evidence: Supported by pre-tone freezing measurements with statistical analysis

claim: Shisa7 KO mice show no significant genotype effect in anxiety-related tasks.
source: Finally, Shisa7 KO mice were tested in several anxiety-related tasks, such as open field, elevated plus maze and dark-light box, in which no significant genotype effect was observed (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by multiple anxiety test data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2

claim: Mice lacking Shisa7 show reduced acquisition and expression of contextual fear memory but no difference in auditory fear learning or anxiety.
source: Thus, we conclude that mice lacking the Shisa7 protein show reduced acquisition and expression of a contextual fear memory, but no difference in auditory fear learning or anxiety.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on multiple behavioral experiments

claim: Shisa7 is part of native hippocampal AMPAR complexes with unique characteristics compared to Shisa9 and Shisa6.
source: We identified Shisa7 as part of native hippocampal AMPAR complexes with unique characteristics compared with the Shisa9 and Shisa6 members of this protein family (Figure 8; Supplementary file 1 [Klaassen et al., 2016]).
evidence: Summary statement based on multiple experimental findings and comparison to cited work

claim: Physical association of Shisa7 with GluA proteins modulates receptor properties in vitro by increasing AMPAR desensitization.
source: Physical association of Shisa7 with the pore-forming GluA proteins modulates receptor properties in vitro by increasing AMPAR desensitization, lowering the steady state current and slowing down recovery of desensitization.
evidence: Summary of HEK293 cell electrophysiology findings

claim: Physical association of Shisa7 with GluA proteins lowers the steady state current in vitro.
source: Physical association of Shisa7 with the pore-forming GluA proteins modulates receptor properties in vitro by increasing AMPAR desensitization, lowering the steady state current and slowing down recovery of desensitization.
evidence: Summary of HEK293 cell electrophysiology findings

claim: Physical association of Shisa7 with GluA proteins slows down recovery of desensitization in vitro.
source: Physical association of Shisa7 with the pore-forming GluA proteins modulates receptor properties in vitro by increasing AMPAR desensitization, lowering the steady state current and slowing down recovery of desensitization.
evidence: Summary of HEK293 cell electrophysiology findings

claim: Gene deletion of Shisa7 affects rise and decay time of spontaneous AMPAR currents in the hippocampus.
source: Ex vivo, gene deletion of Shisa7 affects rise and decay time of spontaneous and stimulus-evoked AMPAR currents in the hippocampus.
evidence: Summary of mEPSC and eEPSC findings in hippocampal slices

claim: Gene deletion of Shisa7 affects rise and decay time of stimulus-evoked AMPAR currents in the hippocampus.
source: Ex vivo, gene deletion of Shisa7 affects rise and decay time of spontaneous and stimulus-evoked AMPAR currents in the hippocampus.
evidence: Summary of eEPSC findings in hippocampal slices

claim: Shisa7 displays strong biochemical enrichment at the post-synaptic density.
source: Shisa7 displays a strong biochemical enrichment and localization at the post-synaptic density, and interacts with the scaffold protein PSD-95.
evidence: Summary of subcellular fractionation and immunoprecipitation findings

claim: Shisa7 localizes at the post-synaptic density.
source: Shisa7 displays a strong biochemical enrichment and localization at the post-synaptic density, and interacts with the scaffold protein PSD-95.
evidence: Summary of subcellular fractionation and immunocytochemistry findings

claim: Shisa7 interacts with the scaffold protein PSD-95.
source: Shisa7 displays a strong biochemical enrichment and localization at the post-synaptic density, and interacts with the scaffold protein PSD-95.
evidence: Summary of immunoprecipitation and two-hybrid assay findings

claim: Shisa7 is likely involved in experience-dependent changes in synaptic AMPAR expression.
source: Lastly, Shisa7 is likely involved in experience-dependent changes in synaptic AMPAR expression, as AMPAR recruitment during LTP as well as hippocampus-dependent expression of associative memory are strongly affected in Shisa7 KO mice.
evidence: Inferred from LTP and behavioral findings showing impaired AMPAR recruitment and memory

claim: AMPAR recruitment during LTP is strongly affected in Shisa7 KO mice.
source: Lastly, Shisa7 is likely involved in experience-dependent changes in synaptic AMPAR expression, as AMPAR recruitment during LTP as well as hippocampus-dependent expression of associative memory are strongly affected in Shisa7 KO mice.
evidence: Summary of LTP and surface GluA1 findings

claim: Hippocampus-dependent expression of associative memory is strongly affected in Shisa7 KO mice.
source: Lastly, Shisa7 is likely involved in experience-dependent changes in synaptic AMPAR expression, as AMPAR recruitment during LTP as well as hippocampus-dependent expression of associative memory are strongly affected in Shisa7 KO mice.
evidence: Summary of contextual fear conditioning findings

claim: Shisa9 is expressed most prominently in the hippocampus dentate gyrus (DG).

claim: The impact of Shisa7 deletion on plasticity is probably brain region-dependent.
source: It is of interest that only contextual memory was impaired, leaving auditory fear memory intact, whereas Shisa7 is expressed in the hippocampus and amygdala at both the transcript and protein level. Hence, the impact of Shisa7 deletion on plasticity is probably brain region-dependent, which might result from the distinct composition of the associated proteins that reside in different Shisa7-AMPAR complexes.
evidence: Inferred from selective memory deficit despite widespread expression

claim: Shisa7 is functional in AMPAR-containing synapses in the hippocampus.
source: We showed that Shisa7 is functional in AMPAR-containing synapses in the hippocampus and is involved in the fine-tuning of the channel properties of AMPARs, affects hippocampal synaptic plasticity, and takes part in hippocampus-dependent fear memory.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings
